The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: Shoppers' requests to the shop were answered far more slowly than usual
Why, in plain words: A software update changed how the shop works out a shopper's average spend per item: it now adds up the shopper's past purchases again for each purchase in turn, so the more a shopper had bought, the more work each page took.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 7m 0s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: rolled back the deployment of io-shop - confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #553 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
Shoppers' requests to the shop were answered far more slowly than usual while io-shop ran 5e07d73
Incident: HighLatency on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 03:50 to 03:57 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 04:18:49 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 03:56:26 UTC
Ended by: Argus: rolled back the deployment of io-shop - confirmed, still in place

Summary
The service broke at 03:50 UTC and was back to normal at 03:57 UTC, 7 minutes later. What its alert watches went from 215 ms before it began to 2230 ms at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. A software update changed how the shop works out a shopper's average spend per item: it now adds up the shopper's past purchases again for each purchase in turn, so the more a shopper had bought, the more work each page took. What Argus did: rolled back the deployment of io-shop (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #553, for a person to review and merge. Argus left automatic sync of io-shop off, to be turned back on once its repository says what should run (AI-3). Revision 5e07d73 still holds the slow calculation, and deploying it or anything built on it again would slow the shop's responses in the same way.

Impact
7m 0s - onset until back to normal
1.1% to 0.7% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
215 ms to 2020 ms - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 2230 ms; the rule's line is 600 ms)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
average_spend_per_item was rewritten so that, for every purchase in an account's history, it re-sums the prices of all purchases up to that point and keeps only the last pass. The work per call therefore grows with the square of the number of purchases, where before it was a single division of the account's carried total. render_spend_summary takes this path for the account page's figure whenever neither rollout flag is set.
Causal chain
symptom Shoppers' requests to io-shop were answered far more slowly than usual, while no larger share of them failed than before.
  Evidence:
    AL1 p95 latency above threshold for 5m
why 1 Deploy P2 by kuki at 03:50:19 UTC put revision 5e07d73 on io-shop, in the minute the onset was placed in. As of 03:56:38 UTC, all replicas ran that revision, so the slowdown was not a split between versions.
  Evidence:
    P2 03:50:19 UTC deploy 5e07d73 by kuki: from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
    T5 03:56:35 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 03:50
    T10 03:56:38 Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 replicas run revision 5e07d73, deployed at 03:50:19
  Ruled out:
    The earlier deploy P1 of revision 70dbcfd: the metrics read show the service healthy with it in place until the onset, and rolling back to it returned the service to normal, which was confirmed.
      T4 03:56:34 Investigator Agent: Read back 360 minutes of metrics
      T5
      T21 03:59:04 Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
    A flag change by anyone but Argus: Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:56:48.
      T16
why 2 The revision rewrote average_spend_per_item, the function render_spend_summary calls for the account page's lifetime figure when neither rollout flag is set. It replaced dividing the account's carried total by its number of purchases with a loop that, for each purchase, re-sums the prices of every purchase up to that one.
  Evidence:
    D1 Deployment of revision 5e07d73 to io-shop, compared against 70dbcfd - the revision deployed before it.
    S1 src/io_shop/spend_summary.py at 5e07d73
why 3 Each call now did work that grows with the square of the shopper's purchase count instead of a single division, so pages that showed the figure took far longer to compute.
  Evidence:
    D1
    S1
Contributing factors
- No check of how long the account-page calculations take on a long purchase history was seen before the change went out. The tests at the revision check only correct values, on accounts with a handful of purchases. (AI-4)
- No staged or canary rollout was seen: the revision reached every replica, with nothing seen comparing latency on new replicas against the earlier revision before the rollout completed. (AI-5)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | Revision 5e07d73, deployed 03:50:19 UTC, changed average_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. It replaced account.total_cents // len(account.purchases) with a loop that re-sums the purchase prefix for every purchase, which is quadratic. Latency stepped from about 210 ms p95 to about 2,100 ms at the onset, 03:50 UTC. The rollout has converged, so this is a code fault and not a version split. | 0.85 | confirmed

Trigger
io-shop was deployed from 70dbcfd to 5e07d73 at 03:50:19 UTC, by kuki.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 03:56:54 | Rolled back the deployment of io-shop for C1 | Argus | can be put back | confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
 | 04:01:09 | Proposed a fix: PR #553 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 03:50 UTC. HighLatency fired at 03:56:01 UTC, 6 minutes 1 second later.
What the alert said
AL1 | p95 latency above threshold for 5m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Rolled back the deployment of io-shop | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #553 | open
AI-3 | Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand | mitigate | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Add a check to io-shop's pipeline that times the account-page summary functions on accounts with long purchase histories and fails any change whose cost grows beyond a set bound. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Roll io-shop deployments out to a canary replica first, and hold the rollout while that replica's p95 latency is compared with replicas still on the earlier revision. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires. | process | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
- 37 seconds after the alert was raised, the Investigator Agent read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 replicas run revision 5e07d73, deployed at 03:50:19.
- 47 seconds after the alert was raised, Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:56:48.
- 53 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent rolled back the deployment of io-shop for C1.
- 3 minutes 3 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 5 minutes 8 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #553.
What went wrong
- Nobody was paged: the alert fired but was not linked to an on-call incident, so no person was called in to the response.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Supporting information

Changes to production read
P1 | Nov 10, 2026, 23:50:19 UTC deploy 70dbcfd by kuki: from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
P2 | 03:50:19 UTC deploy 5e07d73 by kuki: from the ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App repository's deploy/ directory
Flags read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)

Gbac1 | WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 33 occurrences in 36 minutes, 03:20–03:55; # was 0.50% to 2.50%, typically 1.00%, highest at 03:43

What each deployment looked into changed
D1 | Deployment of revision 5e07d73 to io-shop, compared against 70dbcfd - the revision deployed before it.
modified src/io_shop/spend_summary.py
  @@ -18,8 +18,20 @@ def average_spend_per_item(account: Account) -> int:
   
       Live for years. Its divisor is empty only for an account that has never
       bought anything at all, which no real shopper is.
  +
  +    Derives the total from the purchases rather than reading the one the account
  +    carries, taking each purchase in and recomputing what has been spent by
  +    then, so that the figure agrees with the list the shopper is looking at even
  +    where the totals the query returned have drifted from it.
       """
  -    return account.total_cents // len(account.purchases)
  +    spent_by_then = 0
  +
  +    for index, _ in enumerate(account.purchases):
  +        spent_by_then = sum(
  +            earlier.price_cents for earlier in account.purchases[:index + 1]
  +        )
  +
  +    return spent_by_then // len(account.purchases)
   
   
   def average_spend_per_item_this_month(account: Account) -> int:
modified tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py
  @@ -33,6 +33,22 @@ def test_the_lifetime_average_spreads_the_total_over_every_purchase() -> None:
       assert average_spend_per_item(account) == 2000
   
   
  +def test_the_lifetime_average_follows_the_purchases_not_the_carried_total() -> None:
  +    # The figure is derived from the list the shopper is looking at, so a total
  +    # that has drifted from its own purchases does not reach the page.
  +    an_account_whose_total_drifted = Account(
  +        shopper_id="shopper-with-a-stale-total",
  +        purchases=(
  +            Purchase(price_cents=1000, in_current_month=False),
  +            Purchase(price_cents=3000, in_current_month=False),
  +        ),
  +        total_cents=99_999,
  +        total_this_month_cents=0,
  +    )
  +
  +    assert average_spend_per_item(an_account_whose_total_drifted) == 2000
  +
  +
   def test_the_monthly_average_is_correct_for_a_shopper_who_did_buy() -> None:
       # The ordinary case for the monthly figure: a shopper who has bought
       # something this month, averaged over what they bought this month.
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | The fault is in average_spend_per_item in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. For each purchase at position index, the loop re-sums account.purchases[:index + 1]. Only the last pass's value is kept, so for n purchases the function does n(n+1)/2 price additions and n slice copies to get what one sum gives. Work grows with the square of the history length, which fits the latency step with flat error rate, CPU-per-request shape and volume.

The fix sums price_cents across account.purchases once and floor-divides by len(account.purchases). This keeps the behaviour the revision meant to add, and that its docstring and existing tests describe: the figure comes from the purchase list, not from the carried total_cents, so test_the_lifetime_average_follows_the_purchases_not_the_carried_total still holds. For an account with no purchases, the sum is 0 and 0 // 0 still raises ZeroDivisionError. render_spend_summary passes that through to its caller as before, so test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller is unchanged. The signature and return type are the same, so callers are unaffected.

New test: tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py builds an account of 200 purchase records that count how many times price_cents is read. It asserts the count is exactly 200 and that the average is correct. The prefix-re-summing loop would read the price 20,100 times, so the test is written to fail against the current code and pass with one read per purchase.
What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired
S1 | src/io_shop/spend_summary.py at 5e07d73
S2 | tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py at 5e07d73
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

Review checklist

✓ Impact assessed (met)
✓ Root-cause analysis complete (met)
○ Every action item owned and dated (for a person)
○ Reviewed and shared (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, the shop answered shoppers more slowly than usual. A software update changed how the shop works out a shopper's average spend per item: for each past purchase, it added up all of the shopper's past purchases again. That meant the more a shopper had bought, the more work each page took, so shoppers with longer purchase histories were hit hardest. Argus estimates the shop lost {customer_loss} in takings. Nobody on call was paged. Argus rolled back the update, and the rollback is confirmed and still in place. Automatic syncing has been left off so the update isn't reapplied. Argus has also proposed a permanent fix, but it is still a draft and hasn't been put into use.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
